lessons.title: Nutrient Requirements for Different Stages of Fattening
lessons.body:
Fattening steers goes through three stages: starter (first 30 days), grower (next 60 days), and finisher (last 30-60 days). Each stage needs different amounts of energy, protein, and minerals. In Africa, most steers start at 200-250 kg and finish at 400-450 kg. During the starter stage, give 1.5-2 kg of concentrate per day plus free-choice hay. The concentrate should have 14-16% crude protein (CP) and 70-75% total digestible nutrients (TDN). This helps the rumen adjust to grain and builds appetite.

In the grower stage, increase concentrate to 3-4 kg per day. The diet should have 12-14% CP and 72-76% TDN. This is when the steer builds muscle and frame. Use locally available energy feeds like maize, sorghum, or millet. Mix with protein sources like cottonseed cake or groundnut cake. Always provide clean water and mineral licks.

During the finisher stage, push energy to 80-85% TDN and drop protein to 10-12% CP. Give 5-7 kg of concentrate per day. This stage adds fat and marbling. Too much protein at this stage is wasteful and expensive. Watch for acidosis: if the steer goes off feed, reduce grain and add roughage.

A simple rule: a 300 kg steer eats about 2.5-3% of its body weight in dry matter daily. So a 300 kg steer needs 7.5-9 kg of feed dry matter. Adjust based on body condition. In hot African climates, feed early morning and evening when it's cool. Always provide shade and water. Weigh your steers every 30 days to track gain. Aim for 0.8-1.2 kg gain per day. If gain is below 0.5 kg, check feed quality and health.

lessons.title: Energy Feeds: Grains and By-Products
lessons.body:
Energy feeds are the fuel for fattening. In Africa, the most common energy feeds are maize, sorghum, millet, and their by-products. Maize is king: it has about 85% TDN and 8-9% CP. Crack or grind maize to improve digestion. Whole kernels often pass through undigested. For a 300 kg steer, 3-4 kg of cracked maize per day is a good starting point. But maize is also human food, so use by-products where possible.

Maize bran (also called maize offal or pollard) is a great energy feed. It has 70-75% TDN and 8-10% CP. It is cheaper than whole maize and widely available from local mills. Rice bran is another option: 65-70% TDN and 10-12% CP. But rice bran can go rancid quickly, so store it dry and use within two weeks. Wheat bran has 65-70% TDN and 14-16% CP, making it both energy and protein. It is excellent for fattening.

Sorghum and millet are drought-tolerant and grow well in dry areas. They have similar energy to maize (80-85% TDN) but slightly lower protein (7-9% CP). Use them when maize is expensive. Molasses is a liquid energy feed with 50-60% TDN. It is cheap but can cause scours if overfed. Limit molasses to 1-1.5 kg per day for a 300 kg steer. Mix it with dry feed to prevent sticking.

Cassava peels and chips are energy feeds in West and Central Africa. They have 60-70% TDN but low protein (2-3% CP). Never feed raw cassavaâit contains cyanide. Dry or ensile it first. Always introduce any new energy feed slowly over 7-10 days to avoid digestive upset. Store grains in dry, raised cribs to prevent aflatoxin from mold.

lessons.title: Protein Sources: Oilseed Meals and Legumes
lessons.body:
Protein builds muscle and is critical in the starter and grower stages. The best oilseed meals in Africa are cottonseed cake, groundnut cake, sunflower cake, and soybean meal. Cottonseed cake has 30-35% CP. It is widely available in West and East Africa. But it contains gossypol, which can be toxic. Limit cottonseed cake to 1-1.5 kg per day for a 300 kg steer. Groundnut cake has 40-45% CP and is very palatable. It is excellent but can be expensive. Sunflower cake has 28-32% CP and is a good mid-range option.

Soybean meal is the gold standard with 44-48% CP. It is often imported or expensive, so use it sparinglyâ0.5-1 kg per day is enough to balance a ration. Always heat-treat raw soybeans to destroy trypsin inhibitors. Legume forages are another protein source. Lucerne (alfalfa) hay has 15-18% CP. Lablab, cowpea, and groundnut haulms are common in Africa. Groundnut haulms have 10-12% CP and are very digestible. Use them as part of the roughage.

For a 300 kg steer in the grower stage, aim for 12-14% CP in the total diet. If you feed 3 kg of maize (9% CP) and 4 kg of hay (8% CP), you need about 0.5 kg of cottonseed cake (32% CP) to reach 13% CP. Mix well. Protein is expensive, so do not overfeed. Excess protein is excreted as urea, wasting money and polluting the environment. In the finisher stage, drop protein to 10-12% CP. Too much protein can make the meat dark and reduce fat deposition. Store oilseed cakes in dry, cool places to prevent mold and rancidity.

lessons.title: Forages: Hay, Silage, and Pasture
lessons.body:
Forages are the backbone of ruminant nutrition. They provide fiber, which keeps the rumen healthy. In Africa, common forages include natural pasture, crop residues (maize stover, sorghum stover, rice straw), and planted forages (elephant grass, Rhodes grass, lucerne). Hay is dried forage. Good hay is green, leafy, and smells sweet. It should have 8-12% CP and 50-60% TDN. Make hay when grass is young and before flowering. Dry it in the sun for 2-3 days, then store under cover. Poor hay is brown, stemmy, and dustyâit has little feed value.

Silage is fermented forage. It is made by chopping green forage, packing it tightly in a pit or silo, and covering it to exclude air. Maize silage is the best, with 65-70% TDN and 8-10% CP. Sorghum silage is also good. To make silage, chop maize at dough stage (when kernels are soft but not dry). Add molasses if the crop is too dry. Pack in layers, press out air, and seal with plastic. After 3-4 weeks, it is ready. Good silage smells like vinegar, not manure. Feed 5-10 kg per steer per day.

Pasture is the cheapest forage. Rotational grazing improves yield and prevents parasites. Allow grass to grow to 20-30 cm before grazing, and graze down to 10 cm. Do not overgraze. In dry seasons, pasture quality drops. Supplement with hay, silage, or concentrate. Crop residues are abundant after harvest. Maize stover has 4-6% CP and 45-50% TDN. Treat with urea to improve digestibility: mix 4 kg urea in 100 liters water, sprinkle on 100 kg stover, cover for 2 weeks. This raises CP to 8-10%. Always provide forages free-choice to steers. They need at least 1.5-2% of body weight in forage dry matter daily.

lessons.title: Minerals, Vitamins, and Feed Additives
lessons.body:
Minerals and vitamins are needed in small amounts but are critical for health and growth. The most important minerals for fattening steers are calcium (Ca), phosphorus (P), salt (NaCl), and trace minerals like zinc, copper, and selenium. In Africa, soils are often deficient in phosphorus and selenium. Provide a mineral lick free-choice. A good lick should have 8-10% Ca, 6-8% P, and 20-25% salt. If you cannot buy a commercial lick, mix your own: 40% limestone, 30% bone meal, 20% salt, 10% trace mineral premix. Offer it in a wooden box or trough.

Vitamins A, D, and E are the most important. Green forage provides vitamin A precursors (carotene). If steers are on dry feed for more than 2 months, inject vitamin A or add a supplement. Vitamin D is made by sunlight, so steers in sunny Africa rarely need extra. Vitamin E is in green feed and grains. Feed additives are non-nutrient substances that improve growth or health. Common additives include ionophores (like monensin), which improve feed efficiency by 5-10%. They also reduce bloat and acidosis. Use according to label directionsâusually 20-30 g per ton of feed.

Probiotics (live yeast) can stabilize the rumen and improve fiber digestion. Add 5-10 g per steer per day. Buffers like sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) help prevent acidosis when feeding high grain. Add 0.5-1% of the concentrate. Urea can be used as a non-protein nitrogen source for ruminants, but never feed more than 1% of the diet or 0.3 g per kg body weight. Too much urea is toxic. Mix urea thoroughly with feed. Never feed urea to non-ruminants. Always provide clean waterâsteers drink 30-50 liters per day. Store minerals and additives in dry, labeled containers away from children and animals.

lessons.title: Feed Analysis and Quality Assessment
lessons.body:
You cannot manage what you do not measure. Feed analysis tells you the nutrient content of your feeds. The most important measures are dry matter (DM), crude protein (CP), total digestible nutrients (TDN), and fiber (NDF). You can send samples to a laboratory, but simple on-farm tests can help. For dry matter, weigh a sample, dry it in an oven at 60Â°C for 24 hours, and weigh again. The difference is moisture. Most feeds are 85-90% DM when air-dry. For protein, you need a lab. But you can estimate: oilseed cakes are high (30-45% CP), cereals are medium (8-12% CP), and straws are low (3-6% CP).

Physical assessment is quick and free. Good hay is green, leafy, and smells fresh. Bad hay is brown, moldy, or dusty. Good silage smells like vinegar and is not slimy. Good grain is dry, clean, and free of mold. Moldy grain may contain aflatoxin, which is poisonous. Test for aflatoxin with a simple kit if available. For concentrates, look for uniform particle size and no clumping. Smell for rancidity in oilseed cakes. Taste a small amount of mineral mixâit should be salty but not bitter.

A simple tool is the Penn State Forage Particle Separator. It has three screens that separate feed into long, medium, and fine particles. For fattening steers, you want 10-20% long particles, 30-50% medium, and 40-60% fine. Too many fines cause acidosis; too many long particles reduce intake. You can make a homemade version with three boxes with different mesh sizes. Also, weigh your steers monthly. If average daily gain is below 0.8 kg, your feed quality is likely poor. Adjust the ration. Keep records of feed purchases, weights, and gains. This helps you identify which feeds give the best return. Always buy feed from trusted suppliers and store it properly.

quiz.q: What is the recommended crude protein (CP) percentage for the starter stage of fattening steers?
quiz.explanation: The starter stage requires 14-16% CP to help the rumen adjust and build appetite.

quiz.q: During which stage should you increase concentrate to 5-7 kg per day?
quiz.explanation: The finisher stage pushes energy with 5-7 kg of concentrate per day to add fat.

quiz.q: What is the target average daily gain for fattening steers?
quiz.explanation: Aim for 0.8-1.2 kg gain per day; below 0.5 kg indicates problems.

quiz.q: How much dry matter does a 300 kg steer eat per day?
quiz.explanation: Steers eat about 2.5-3% of body weight in dry matter, so 7.5-9 kg for 300 kg.

quiz.q: Which feed is highest in total digestible nutrients (TDN)?
quiz.explanation: Maize has about 85% TDN, higher than rice bran (65-70%), wheat bran (65-70%), and molasses (50-60%).

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended amount of molasses per day for a 300 kg steer?
quiz.explanation: Limit molasses to 1-1.5 kg per day to avoid scours.

quiz.q: Which energy feed contains cyanide and must be dried or ensiled before feeding?
quiz.explanation: Raw cassava contains cyanide; drying or ensiling reduces it to safe levels.

quiz.q: What is the crude protein content of cottonseed cake?
quiz.explanation: Cottonseed cake has 30-35% CP but contains gossypol, so limit intake.

quiz.q: Which protein source is considered the gold standard with 44-48% CP?
quiz.explanation: Soybean meal has 44-48% CP and is highly digestible but often expensive.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended amount of cottonseed cake per day for a 300 kg steer?
quiz.explanation: Limit cottonseed cake to 1-1.5 kg per day due to gossypol toxicity.

quiz.q: Which legume forage has 15-18% CP and is also called alfalfa?
quiz.explanation: Lucerne (alfalfa) hay has 15-18% CP and is an excellent legume forage.

quiz.q: In the finisher stage, what should the crude protein level be?
quiz.explanation: Drop protein to 10-12% CP in the finisher stage to avoid waste and dark meat.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for good hay?
quiz.explanation: Good hay is dried to 15-20% moisture to prevent mold.

quiz.q: Which forage is best for making silage?
quiz.explanation: Maize silage has 65-70% TDN and 8-10% CP, making it the best silage crop.

quiz.q: How long does silage need to ferment before feeding?
quiz.explanation: Silage is ready after 3-4 weeks of fermentation.

quiz.q: What is the crude protein content of maize stover?
quiz.explanation: Maize stover has 4-6% CP and 45-50% TDN.

quiz.q: How can you improve the digestibility of maize stover?
quiz.explanation: Urea treatment raises CP to 8-10% and improves digestibility.

quiz.q: Which mineral is often deficient in African soils and must be provided in a lick?
quiz.explanation: Phosphorus is commonly deficient in African soils, so mineral licks should include it.

quiz.q: What percentage of salt should a good mineral lick contain?
quiz.explanation: A good mineral lick has 20-25% salt to encourage intake.

quiz.q: Which vitamin is made by sunlight and rarely needs supplementation in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin D is synthesized by sunlight, so steers in sunny Africa rarely need extra.

quiz.q: What is the maximum safe level of urea in a steer's diet?
quiz.explanation: Urea should not exceed 1% of the diet or 0.3 g per kg body weight to avoid toxicity.

quiz.q: What do ionophores like monensin do?
quiz.explanation: Ionophores improve feed efficiency by 5-10% and reduce acidosis.

quiz.q: How much water does a fattening steer drink per day?
quiz.explanation: Steers drink 30-50 liters of clean water daily.

quiz.q: What is the first step in feed analysis on the farm?
quiz.explanation: Dry matter is the simplest and most important measure, done by drying a sample.

quiz.q: What does a Penn State Forage Particle Separator measure?
quiz.explanation: It separates feed into long, medium, and fine particles to assess rumen health.

quiz.q: What percentage of long particles is ideal in a fattening steer's diet?
quiz.explanation: 10-20% long particles help maintain rumen function without reducing intake.

quiz.q: What is a sign of good silage?
quiz.explanation: Good silage smells like vinegar and is not slimy or foul-smelling.

quiz.q: Which feed is most likely to contain aflatoxin if moldy?
quiz.explanation: Moldy maize can produce aflatoxin, which is poisonous to steers.

quiz.q: What should you do if average daily gain is below 0.5 kg?
options: B) Check feed quality and health
quiz.explanation: Poor gain indicates problems with feed quality, health, or management.

quiz.q: How often should you weigh your steers to track gain?
quiz.explanation: Weighing every 30 days helps track average daily gain and adjust rations.
